opus-5.5.text:
So, I think the key insight is that you don't want to use deep learning to generate programs directly, token by token. That's the approach where you treat program synthesis as just another sequence prediction problem, and it doesn't generalize well, because the model is just interpolating over the programs it has seen. What you want instead is to use deep learning as a kind of intuition engine that guides a discrete search process.

If you think about how humans solve ARC tasks, there are really two modes of cognition at play. There's the fast, intuitive, pattern-matching mode, where you look at the grid and immediately get a feel for what's going on: "this is about objects," "this is about symmetry," "something is being counted here." And then there's the slower, deliberate, step-by-step reasoning mode, where you actually verify a hypothesis and work out the exact transformation. Deep learning is great at the first kind, and discrete program search is great at the second kind. The trick is to merge them.

So concretely, if I had a year, I would start by building a really good domain-specific language for ARC, one that captures the core knowledge priors: objectness, basic geometry and topology, numbers and counting, goal-directedness. That DSL is your search space. The problem with naive program search is combinatorial explosion. As soon as your programs get a little bit deep, the space of possible programs becomes astronomically large, and brute force just doesn't scale.

That's where deep learning comes in. You would train a model to look at a task, the input-output pairs, and output a probability distribution over which primitives are likely to be relevant, or which subprograms are likely to appear, or how promising a partial program is. Basically you use the neural network to prune the search tree and to make the branching factor manageable. It's like how AlphaGo or AlphaZero uses a value network and a policy network to guide tree search: you're not searching blindly, you're searching with intuition.

Another important element would be building up a library of reusable abstractions over time. When you solve a task, you should extract the useful subroutines from the solution and add them back into your DSL, so that the system gets better and more efficient as it sees more tasks. That's very much in the spirit of DreamCoder, from Kevin Ellis and Josh Tenenbaum's group. This is what I mean when I talk about intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency: you want a system that accumulates abstractions and reuses them, so that each new problem becomes cheaper to solve.

And I'd also look at the data side. ARC only has a few hundred training tasks, which isn't a lot to train a neural network on. So I would invest in generating a lot of synthetic tasks, by sampling programs from the DSL and running them on generated inputs. That gives you a large dataset of program and input-output pairs that you can use to train the guiding model. The caveat is that you have to be careful about distribution: the synthetic tasks have to be diverse and meaningful enough that the intuition you learn actually transfers to the real tasks.

So in summary: a DSL grounded in core knowledge, a neural network trained to provide intuition about which parts of program space to explore, discrete search to actually find and verify programs, and a mechanism for abstraction learning so the system builds up its own library over time. I genuinely think that kind of hybrid is the most promising path, not just for ARC but for getting toward more general intelligence. Pure deep learning alone won't get you there, and pure discrete search alone won't get you there either. You need both.

r001.rationale: It rejects generating programs token by token and says that approach generalizes poorly.

r002.rationale: It proposes an ARC-specific DSL, but does not represent programs as graphs of operators.

r003.rationale: It describes using a neural network to prune the search tree and guide the search.

r004.rationale: It recommends neural networks to guide program search but does not specifically mention LLMs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, if I had a year to spend entirely on ARC, I think the first thing I'd do is resist the temptation to just throw a big transformer at it end-to-end. ARC was designed specifically so that doesn't work. Every task is novel, you get two or three examples, and the thing you're being asked to do is not recognize a pattern you've seen before, it's synthesize a new program on the fly. So the problem is fundamentally one of search, and the question becomes: how do you make that search tractable?

The way I think about it, there are two kinds of abstraction. There's value-centric abstraction, which is what deep learning is very good at: you have a continuous space, you compare things by distance, you interpolate. And there's program-centric abstraction, which is discrete, it's about structure, it's about matching graphs of operations. ARC lives almost entirely in the second regime. But the second regime is combinatorially explosive. If you do pure brute-force search over a domain-specific language, you hit a wall very quickly, because the space of programs grows exponentially with program length. So the role of deep learning, in my view, is not to solve the task. It's to guide the search. It's intuition about the shape of the solution.

So concretely, I'd start by building a good DSL. That's actually a lot of the work, and I don't think people take it seriously enough. You want a set of primitives that captures the core knowledge priors ARC assumes: objectness, counting, basic geometry and topology, goal-directedness, symmetry. You want the DSL to be expressive enough that most tasks have short programs in it, because search cost is dominated by program depth. And you want it to be compositional in a clean way, so that partial programs have meaning you can evaluate.

Then the deep learning piece. There are a few places you can inject it. One is as a prior over program structure: given the input-output pairs, predict which primitives are likely to be relevant, or predict a distribution over the first few nodes of the program. That alone cuts the branching factor enormously. Another is as a learned heuristic for partial-program evaluation: you've applied three operations, you're not at the output yet, how promising is this intermediate state? That's a value function, and it's something a neural network can learn from lots of search traces. And a third, which I find quite interesting, is learning the DSL itself over time. You run search, you find solutions, you notice recurring sub-programs, and you compress them into new primitives. That's a form of abstraction generation, and it's probably closer to what human programmers actually do.

The hard part, honestly, is the training data. ARC gives you a few hundred tasks. That's nothing for a neural network. So you'd need to generate synthetic tasks, which means you need a generative model over tasks, which is itself kind of an ARC-shaped problem. I'd probably spend a lot of the year on that: building a task generator that samples programs from the DSL, applies them to procedurally generated grids, and produces training pairs. The risk is that your generator only produces tasks that look like your DSL, and then your system is just learning to invert your own generator. You have to be careful to evaluate on the real ARC set and to be honest when the synthetic distribution doesn't transfer.

And then the last thing I'd say is, I'd be very interested in test-time adaptation. The thing that's special about ARC is that each task gives you a few demonstrations, and a human uses those demonstrations to actively reason. Most deep learning systems do all their learning at training time and then just do a forward pass. I think you want to do some real computation at test time: run search, maybe fine-tune or adapt the guiding network on the demonstrations themselves, iterate. Intelligence, to me, is efficiency at acquiring new skills. So the metric I'd care about is not just how many tasks you solve, it's how much search you had to do per task, how much of the prior you were able to leverage. If you get that right, I think you'd learn something genuinely new about what it means to build systems that can handle novelty, which is really the whole point of ARC in the first place.

r001.rationale: It rejects an end-to-end transformer and favors search, but does not clearly address token-by-token code generation.

r002.rationale: It describes program-centric abstraction as matching graphs of operations.

r003.rationale: It frames synthesis as search through partial programs, with branching factors and successive program nodes, which conveys tree search.

r004.rationale: It recommends deep learning to guide program search, including learned priors and heuristics, but does not specifically mention LLMs.

astra-6.text:
I would probably start by working on the program representation. What are the primitives you need to express solutions to these tasks? You want a language that makes it easy to talk about objects, spatial relationships, transformations, repetition, and so on. If the representation is wrong, the search becomes very difficult, regardless of how good your neural network is.

Then I would build a program synthesis system that can actually solve some tasks through search, even if it’s very slow. That gives you a baseline, and it gives you data. You can generate programs, execute them to produce input-output examples, and train a deep learning model to guide the search back toward the programs that explain those examples.

The role of deep learning here would be to provide intuition: given this task and this partial program, what should I try next? Which operations are likely to be useful? The symbolic part gives you a way to construct a precise solution and check whether it matches the demonstrations.

A major challenge would be making sure your generated training tasks are sufficiently diverse. You don’t want to build a generator that just reproduces the particular problems you’ve already seen. You want the system to acquire reusable abstractions and then compose them in new ways.

So I would spend that year iterating between the representation, the search procedure, and the learned guidance. I would want to measure whether learning actually lets you solve unfamiliar tasks with less search, rather than merely making you better at recognizing familiar task templates.

r001.rationale: The response discusses program representation and search, but does not argue against generating code token by token.

r002.rationale: It proposes a language with useful primitives, but does not represent programs as graphs of operators.

r003.rationale: It proposes search over programs, but does not characterize that search as tree search.

r004.rationale: It says a deep learning model should guide search using partial programs and likely operations, but does not identify LLMs as the guiding models.

sol-6.1.text:
I would probably start with a fairly conventional program synthesis system. You need a domain-specific language for expressing transformations of grids, and you need a search procedure that can compose these primitives into programs that explain the examples. The important question is then: where can deep learning help make that search tractable?

One place is perception. You look at a grid and identify objects, symmetries, repetitions, relationships between objects. Those are useful abstractions for the program to operate on. Another place is guiding the search itself: given the input-output examples and a partial program, predict which operations are worth trying next. You're using a neural network to provide a prior over programs, while the symbolic system checks whether a candidate actually works.

I would spend a lot of time on the language and on generating training tasks. You can sample programs, generate examples from them, and train a model to recover the programs. But there's a danger there: your model may become very good at the distribution you've constructed and still fail on a new kind of task. So you need to evaluate whether it can recombine familiar concepts in unfamiliar ways.

The objective wouldn't be to have a network directly predict the output grid. It would be to have a system that can construct a new program for each task, using the few examples available. Deep learning would supply useful intuitions about where to search, and program synthesis would turn those intuitions into an explicit solution.

r001.rationale: The response favors program synthesis over direct output-grid prediction, but does not argue against token-by-token code generation.

r002.rationale: It describes composing primitives into programs, but does not propose representing programs as graphs of operators.

r003.rationale: It mentions a search procedure, but does not characterize synthesis as tree search.

r004.rationale: It proposes using a neural network to guide program search, but does not identify LLMs as the models to use.
